parts.title: Booking a school trip to a farm
parts.context: A teacher phones a farm to book a school visit.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Part 1. You will hear a teacher phoning a farm to book a school visit. First, you have some time to look at questions 1 to 5.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: You will see that there is an example that has been done for you. On this occasion only, the conversation relating to this will be played first.

script.speaker: greg
script.text: Good morning, Oakfield Farm, Greg speaking.

script.speaker: delaney
script.text: Good morning. I'm a teacher at a primary school, and I'd like to bring my class to see the farm. Do you do school visits?

script.speaker: greg
script.text: We do, and they're very popular. Let me take some details and then I'll tell you what we offer.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: The caller is from a primary school, so 'primary' has been written in the space. Now we shall begin. You should answer the questions as you listen, because you will not hear the recording a second time. Listen carefully and answer questions 1 to 5.

script.speaker: greg
script.text: Could I have your name, please?

script.speaker: delaney
script.text: It's Rosie Delaney, that's D-E-L-A-N-E-Y.

script.speaker: greg
script.text: Thank you, Ms Delaney. How many children are you bringing?

script.speaker: delaney
script.text: There are thirty-five in the class, but three of them will be away on a family trip that week, so thirty-two.

script.speaker: greg
script.text: Fine. We have two possible dates in May. Would the Thursday the twenty-second suit you?

script.speaker: delaney
script.text: Yes, that would be perfect. The twenty-ninth is half-term, so I couldn't have done that one.

script.speaker: greg
script.text: Good. We open at nine, but most schools arrive at ten, so that the children don't have to get up too early. Is ten all right?

script.speaker: delaney
script.text: Ten is ideal. And what will the children actually do?

script.speaker: greg
script.text: There's a tractor ride round the fields, a visit to the dairy, and in May it's the lambs. The children can help to feed them, and that's always the favourite part.

script.speaker: delaney
script.text: Wonderful. They'll love that.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Before you hear the rest of the conversation, you have some time to look at questions 6 to 10.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Now listen and answer questions 6 to 10.

script.speaker: greg
script.text: Now, the cost. It's normally eight pounds a child, but we give schools a discount, so it's seven pounds.

script.speaker: delaney
script.text: That's reasonable. Do the teachers pay?

script.speaker: greg
script.text: No, teachers and helpers come free. And one more thing: the farm can be very muddy, so please tell the children to wear boots. They don't need hats, but a waterproof coat is a good idea.

script.speaker: delaney
script.text: I'll tell them. Where do we eat lunch?

script.speaker: greg
script.text: There are picnic tables outside, but if it rains you're welcome to use the barn. It's dry, and it has plenty of room.

script.speaker: delaney
script.text: That's helpful. Is there anything else I should know?

script.speaker: greg
script.text: Every child gets a free badge to take home, so they'll have something to remember the day. And I'll post you a booking form with the details. Could you sign it and return it by Friday, please, so that we can keep the date for you?

script.speaker: delaney
script.text: Certainly. I'll do it this week. Thank you so much for your help.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: That is the end of Part 1. You now have half a minute to check your answers.

parts.title: Welcome to a new university
parts.context: A member of staff shows new students round the campus.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Part 2. You will hear a member of staff welcoming new students to a university. First, you have some time to look at questions 11 to 15.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions 11 to 15.

script.speaker: farley
script.text: Good morning, everyone, and welcome to Brookfield University. I'm Sandra Farley, from the student services team, and this morning I'll show you where everything is. Please look at the map. We're at the main gate, at the bottom, and the library is at the top of the main path, straight ahead of you.

script.speaker: farley
script.text: Let's start with the places you'll need in your first week. Just inside the gate, on the right of the path and next to the car park, is the health centre. You should register there as soon as you can.

script.speaker: farley
script.text: Directly opposite the health centre, on the left of the path, is the bookshop. Students get ten percent off, so do remember to take your student card.

script.speaker: farley
script.text: Further up on the left, beside the lake, is the sports hall. It has a swimming pool and a climbing wall, and membership is free in your first term.

script.speaker: farley
script.text: Opposite the sports hall, on the right of the path, is the student union. That's where all the clubs and societies are based, so it's the place to go if you'd like to join something.

script.speaker: farley
script.text: Finally, on the left of the library, at the top of the map, you'll find the lecture theatres. Your timetables tell you which one to go to. On the far right of the map is the new science centre, but it isn't open yet, so you won't be using it this year.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Before you hear the rest of the talk, you have some time to look at questions 16 to 20.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Now listen and answer questions 16 to 20.

script.speaker: farley
script.text: Now, a few practical points. Your student card is the key to almost everything, and it can be collected from the library desk, not the union as some of you may have heard. Please bring a passport or driving licence as proof of identity.

script.speaker: farley
script.text: A word about the library. It's open until midnight during term, and this year there's a new silent floor on the top level, for people who find the other floors too busy. There aren't any more computers than last year, but there are more power sockets for your own laptops.

script.speaker: farley
script.text: The campus bus into town leaves from the main gate every ten minutes, and it's free for students. The last bus is at eleven, so if you're out later you'll need a taxi.

script.speaker: farley
script.text: About the health centre. You can't see a doctor there unless you're registered, so please don't leave it until you're ill. Registration takes five minutes, and you'll need to fill in a short form.

script.speaker: farley
script.text: And finally, on Friday evening there's a welcome party in the student union, with music and free food, and everyone is invited. It's a great way to meet the people who'll be on your course. Enjoy your first week.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: That is the end of Part 2. You now have half a minute to check your answers.

parts.title: A plan for a student café
parts.context: Two business students discuss the plan for a café on campus.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Part 3. You will hear two business students, Emma and Ravi, discussing a plan for a student café. First, you have some time to look at questions 21 to 25.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions 21 to 25.

script.speaker: emma
script.text: I've put the questionnaire results into a table, Ravi. Out of a hundred and twenty students who answered, ninety said they would use a café on campus, which is three quarters.

script.speaker: ravi
script.text: That's encouraging. But how many said they'd use it more than once a week?

script.speaker: emma
script.text: Only forty, so we shouldn't be too optimistic about sales.

script.speaker: ravi
script.text: What did people say they wanted most?

script.speaker: emma
script.text: Cheap coffee, by a long way. Then healthy food, and then a quiet place to study. Surprisingly, hardly anybody mentioned free wifi, probably because the university already provides it.

script.speaker: ravi
script.text: Our tutor will like that. She said the business plan has to be based on our own research.

script.speaker: emma
script.text: And there's the question about opening hours. Most people want a café that's open in the evening, until nine, but I'm not sure we can afford to pay staff that late.

script.speaker: ravi
script.text: We could open until seven and see how it goes. Now, the location. The students' union has offered us the room next to the bookshop.

script.speaker: emma
script.text: It's a good spot, but I'm worried about the kitchen.

script.speaker: ravi
script.text: Yes, there's no kitchen, only a small sink, so we'd have to prepare everything somewhere else.

script.speaker: emma
script.text: True. There's also the old sports pavilion. It has a kitchen, but it's a long walk from the main buildings.

script.speaker: ravi
script.text: Why don't we go and look at it this week, and then decide?

script.speaker: emma
script.text: Good idea.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Before you hear the rest of the discussion, you have some time to look at questions 26 to 30.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Now listen and answer questions 26 to 30.

script.speaker: emma
script.text: Right, let's go through each part of the plan. The location. We'll look at the pavilion first, but I think we should also ask the university whether we're even allowed to use it.

script.speaker: ravi
script.text: Agreed. The menu next. We planned sandwiches, soup and cakes. Is that enough?

script.speaker: emma
script.text: I'd keep it as it is. A short menu keeps the costs down, and the survey didn't ask for anything else.

script.speaker: ravi
script.text: Prices. We planned to charge two pounds for a coffee, but the campus shop only charges one pound eighty.

script.speaker: emma
script.text: Then we should change ours, or students will go there instead. One pound fifty, perhaps?

script.speaker: ravi
script.text: The opening hours: until seven, as we said. But I'd like to find out what the cafés in town do.

script.speaker: emma
script.text: Good idea. Why don't you visit two of them this week, and see when their customers come?

script.speaker: ravi
script.text: Finally, the name. We've called it 'The Study Break'.

script.speaker: emma
script.text: I'm not sure it's right. I think we should do another survey and let students vote on a name.

script.speaker: ravi
script.text: Fine. Then we'll have plenty to show our tutor on Monday.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: That is the end of Part 3. You now have half a minute to check your answers.

parts.title: Lecture: salt marshes and coastal defence
parts.context: A lecture on why salt marshes matter and how they are managed.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Part 4. You will hear a lecture about salt marshes and coastal defence. First, you have some time to look at questions 31 to 40.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions 31 to 40.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: Good afternoon. Today's lecture is about salt marshes, which are some of the most valuable, and most overlooked, habitats on our coasts.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: A salt marsh is an area of low-lying land beside the sea that is flooded at high tide and drains at low tide. Because the water is salty, the plants that live there must be able to tolerate salt, and only a few species can. Examples are cord grass and sea lavender.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: Marshes form in sheltered places, such as river mouths, where mud settles out of the water. Pioneer plants colonise the mud, and their roots trap more and more of it, so that the level of the land slowly rises, and new species can move in.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: Why do marshes matter? First, they protect the coast. A marsh a hundred metres wide can reduce the height of waves by up to fifty percent, because the plants slow the water down. That is why engineers now consider marshes to be a cheaper alternative to a concrete sea wall, which is expensive to build and expensive to repair.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: Second, marshes store carbon. The mud is so waterlogged that dead plants decay very slowly, so the carbon stays locked away, sometimes for thousands of years. Per hectare, a salt marsh can store more carbon than a forest.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: Third, they are important for wildlife. Many fish use the marsh as a nursery, and in winter, huge flocks of migrating geese feed there. Without the marsh, they would have nowhere to go.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: Unfortunately, about half of the marshes in Europe have been lost over the last two hundred years, most of them drained so that the land could be used as farmland. Today the main danger is rising sea levels. A marsh can move inland as the sea rises, but not if there is a sea wall behind it, a problem called coastal squeeze.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: One solution is called managed retreat. The sea wall is deliberately moved back, or even removed, so that the sea can flood the land behind it, and a new marsh can form. It is controversial, because farmers lose land, but in several countries it has proved cheaper than keeping the old defences. Next week, we'll look at mangroves.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: That is the end of Part 4. You now have half a minute to check your answers.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: That is the end of the Listening test.
